comments.author: @ThomasMeli
comments.text:
6:15 - Intuitive Diffusion Explanation - I think diffusion models will start to make sense to you once you introduce the idea of blending as a step-by-step process, which learns the patterns in each step and associated them with words in the prompt ("iPhone").  Let’s revisit the blending example with this in mind. In the first step of blending, the components of the iPhone might still be mostly intact, just slightly damaged or bent. Now just go backwards - It’s relatively straightforward to imagine reconstructing the original iPhone from this slightly altered state. In the next step, the phone might be cut a bit—again, you could think about just gluing the parts back together. With each successive step, the damage increases, but simultaneously, the model learns how to reconstruct from a slightly more degraded state back to a more complete form. Each iteration teaches the model both a pattern of "deconstruction" and a pattern of "reconstruction."  

I think the main roadblock you were having had to do with trying to imagine how you could reconstruct a full phone from its fully blended components, but this mental model doesn't include within it the learning that occurs at each  step to go from fully functioning phone to blended pulp of a phone and back again.  If you include that "intelligence" in the process and look at each step as learning representations to go back and forth between the more blended and less blended phone iterations, you can imagine how you could take a phone pulp and reconstruct a phone out of it (at least visually, not materially).

Think of the "noise" or initial state like a set of scattered puzzle pieces that are random enough and numerous enough to form any image we might want if we modify them slightly.  We can dip the puzzle pieces in paint to change their color or cut their edges a little more if we really want to.  The prompt acts as a guide for assembling, cutting, and coloring these pieces. When the model is effectively trained, it learns how to use the prompt to modify and organize  the pieces together, step-by-step, to form a coherent picture.  It learned this from going backwards thousands of times and learning "in general" what to do each step.  

How was that for an intuitive explanation?  I tried to keep all the math out and just give the concept.  Does it make more sense how it is possible and how it works?

comments.author: @WMRhapsodies
comments.text:
About intuitively understanding Diffusion models, here are a couple of ideas, the second one more general and metaphoric, but way more relatable also: 

-1 A Glorified (Intelligent) Denoising Algorithm: a traditional denoising algorithm, knowing nothing about what kind of picture/subject is trying to rebuild, may work by deducing the values of random pixels by other pixels around them. Instead, the Diffusion algorithm knows what kind of picture is trying to rebuild. It will accommodate the random pixel values to a pattern that matches the prompted picture/subject  (in which has been previously thoroughly trained). If you can imagine this process successfully removing the noise from a picture with, say, just a 10% of noise, in order to get a perfectly clear picture (much more efficiently than the "dumb" traditional denoising algorithm), then you must remember that the model has also been trained with labelled pairs of pictures for the previous, intermediate, steps for the prompted subject, like from 20% noise to the 10%, 30% to 20…up to the 100% (I made up the exact values, but you get the idea).

-2 An Acute (Artificial) Case of Pareidolia: which is that thing that happens to us humans when we “see” something very familiar on a random configuration, like to see animal shapes in clouds, or JesusChrist’s face on a toasted slice of bread. The Diffusion algorithm has been trained on lots of patterns (they’r imprinted in the weights of the neural network kind of like the patterns of faces or familiar animals are imprinted in our brain) and by prompting we’r asking the IA to extract those very well known patterns from a totally random configuration.

—

I’m a graphic designer that knows nothing about mathematics or programming (plus, I’m not a native english speaker, in case anything sounds funny). These ideas are made up from watching some technical demonstrations and my own experience working with Stable Diffusion, but I think they may be kind of right since they’v helped me to understand the limitations and nuances of generative art. If @Wes Roth himself or anyone  tech-savvy can elaborate of them (or correcting/criticize them) it would be great. Cheers.

comments.text: Regarding how the denoising in the diffusion model works, I think of it similar to an extreme form of compression. You can take a song in .wav format, and with a good compression algorithm, compress it way down to an .mp3, then in real time, as it is playing, the algorithm tries to recreate the original. If instead, you took input from many songs and compressed them, then added some flexibility in the decompression, you have a music generator. The brain of human artists and musicians works in a similar way. A great artist has seen tens of thousands of drawings, paintings, and reference images, and have arranged their neurons to be able to hallucinate various images, so when you ask them to draw a horse, they can hallucinate an image of a horse in their mind and put it on paper. Same with a musician writing musical notes. They hallucinate a song in their mind using decompression of the compressed imprint of all the music they've heard.

Premises: 
1. The Loab is a product of several signals dropping off into a common, latent, noisy space, but this space is the "outer bullseye" of 100% Pure Noise, more like 80%. The weak signals produce a messy gestalt. 
2. This works from the image end, and produces more noise, 100% pure noise, and then asks for a particular image, cuing an iterative process that can produce the image requested. 
3. Requesting the same still image continuously causes something like a "reversion to the mean", where the noise gradually creeps in, as no *new*, stronger signal is being generated.Only producing a NEW image renews the signal strength.
4, As these images were formed from noise, they're inherently resistant to not only image noise, but are more intensely integrated into temporal sequences. Halt the temporal sequence, the noise starts to creep in. The momentum is everything. You've got yourself a hyperdimensional flywheel.

comments.text: Thermal diffusion is the spread of heat over time. When the heat stops moving, it is considered to be stable. Hence, Stable Diffusion. By reversing this process, you can create images from random noise. The thing that ultimately determines what kind of images are generated are the various patterns that are calculated (i.e. "weights") during the initial training of the model, along with the patterns found in any additions to that model (such as LORAs). To use math as an example, if you trained a neural network by telling it that the expected answer (the resulting image) was supposed to be 7 and you input the numbers 4 and 3, the network would eventually "learn" to add up the numbers 4 and 3 to get 7. After a few thousand iterations using different examples, you would have a neural network model that could perform addition operations. Make sense? Anyway, although doing math seems to be a pretty far cry from creating an image, Stable Diffusion internally creates an array representing the noise during image generation (and during training, fyi) so it can perform the various mathematical operations needed to transform random noise into an image. I hope that explained it well enough.

5:25 I'll give yall a simplified explanation to how Stable Diffusion works.
First of all, there's a reason why it's called "Generative" AI and not just AI, because it's a generator. It doesn't produce anything it doesn't already know thus why there are millions of various finetuned models to download.

The process begins with the deconstruction of an image and the project manager is called "VAE" (Variational Autoencoder), while the VAE is doing that it's creating a cloud of tags called Tokens (words) like arm, hand, sun, sky, grass, bucket, pink, etc... Then the VAE starts to rebuild the images and makes a quality check that dictates if the images looks the same or near identical. If the reconstructed image isn't within spec of the original image it deconstructs the image again and the cycle repeats in Training Steps until the image is identical to the original.
This happens to millions of pictures and all those Tokens gets stored along the deconstructed noise within the model. So whenever you write "cat", the VAE is gonna reach into the bowl of noise and pick up everything that's tagged "cat". So in a way whenever your prompt is a "cat", the output image is literally made from a million cats, that's why a generated image never looks the same if you let the seed number be random.

The second part of it all happens in the Text-Encoder like "CLIP-G" which is responsible for turning your words into tokens, token prediction, forming sentences and understanding the overall complexity of a sentence as a whole. Now, I'm not a scientist or technically versed, but I believe this is a simplistic translation of what's going on.

comments.text: You know how you can see Jesus in a piece of toast? Pareidolia? It's kind of like that. The model steps through sections of the noisy image, looking for any combinations of pixels that seem 'cat' enough. A bit of ear here, a paw there. If you've seen the AI that adds eyes all over an image, it's like that with random cat bits, at this stage. It then zooms out, sampling larger and larger sections of the image. If one section has more ear parts, then the general impression of that area becomes more ear-like. As it's going, it's 'enhancing' the sections which closely match cattiness, adding or subtracting color to pixels around the area to more actively trigger it's cat-part-detector. It knows how to adjust the pixels because of the training data... At a certain stage of adding noise, an ear becomes just a particular curve of dark and light pixels, and this is what it's honing in on. Once the rough details are right, at all scales (so it's not making ears growing out of eyes out of paws, etc...) it produces a 'rough draft' image, which is just the minimum number of pixels to get the idea across. It then repeats that process on this new image, over and over, until you have the level of detail you desire.

@Wes Roth
Here's where I think you were getting confused with your concept of how diffusion works:
When you train a diffusion model, you start with a collection of 'clean' pictures to use as your training data, these pictures have been unaltered. For a training session you would take a clean image, add some random noise and use that as your INPUT to the model. The desired OUTPUT is the original image of the cat, which you still have to compare against. You then alter the weights of the model until the output becomes as close to the original denoised image as it can get. You can apply different random noise to the same image over and over until the model knows how to denoise that particular image regardless of what noise you add. That's the core concept, now add to that many more images of cats, and gradually increase the amount of noise you add to the input images as the model improves, until eventually the model can denoise an image of 100% noise into a cat.

In other words you aren't just teaching the model how to make images noisier and then telling it to do it backwards, you're training a model to denoise images that are so noisy that it requires the model to gain some understanding of the world in order to achieve a high rate of accuracy. So in a sense, the process it uses to create images from pure noise is similar to the process of a human seeing faces in clouds, or staring at the bumps in your ceiling paint as an artistic creative aid.

This wouldn't work for an iphone, because you cant denoise a blended iphone into a functional one, however i wouldn't be surprised if some incredibly useful analog is possible.
